newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea's troubled Jinro streamlining for survival.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea's troubled Jinro streamlining for survival.

text.p: South Korea's troubled Jinro Group on Friday briefed conglomerates and business people on its plan to sell assets ranging from food factories to department stores.
The plan, which Jinro hopes will raise some 1.2 trillion won ($1.34 billion), is being promoted in line with its drive to streamline affiliates, a group executive told Reuters.

"When we complete our restructuring plan and succeed in selling some of our assets, the number of affiliates will be reduced to around 10, or even around seven," said Kim Moon-soo, executive vice president of Jinro Construction Co told Reuters.
Kim led Jinro executives attending the briefing session which drew about 130 people, including officials from other conglomerates and individuals.
Jinro now has 24 affiliates with combined annual sales of 2.2 trillion won in calendar 1996.

Kim said the group would give up food processing, electric cable and other minor manufacturing operations to focus on liquor production, trading, construction, engineering, distribution and environment-related business, including waste treatment.
Aggressive asset sales have been almost unthinkable in the South Korean corporate culture, which has been dominated for the past several decades by greedy expansions, analysts said.
"Jinro's move reflects a change in Korea's overall business environment, and I expect more sellers to follow," said Namuh Rhee, head of research at Dongbang Peregrine Securities.
"More and more companies will be forced to sell assets to make up for their worsening cash flow as a result of falling profits," he said.
Last year South Korean companies saw profits tumble and cash flows deteriorate, largely due to an export slump caused by plunging export prices and a cyclical downturn in the economy.
The sales, which would raise the group's equity-to-asset ratio to 25 percent from the current 4.3 percent, will be through private negotiations, Jinro's Kim said.

Jinro, the nation's 19th largest conglomerate, on Monday announced the asset sales plan to overcome financial troubles. Kim said the troubles were partly the result of a recent string of corporate collapses.
"We are in trouble because financial institutions, mostly non-bank ones, are demanding debt repayments based on rumours that our group is in financial trouble," Kim said.
Jinro has a total of 3.2 trillion won in debts, including about 1.3 trillion owed to non-bank organisations such as merchant banks and mutual savings companies, he said.

Local financial firms, shocked by the collapses of Hanbo Steel Co in January and Sammi Steel Co in March under huge debts, have been cutting back on fresh loans while seeking early repayments of loans.
South Korean commercial banks and other financial institutions recently agreed to form a committee to prevent the collapse of companies fighting cash shortages.
Jinro has already benefited from the move as its major creditor banks have been advising non-bank institutions to refrain from demanding quick debt repayments, Kim said.
"We have fewer loan calls these days after we announced the asset sales plan that was drawn up in consultations with our creditor banks," said Kim.
